**Brigham Young University** (**BYU**) is a [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Provo, Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provo,_Utah "Provo, Utah"), United States. It was founded in 1875 by religious leader [Brigham Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young "Brigham Young") and is the flagship university of the [Church Educational System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Educational_System "Church Educational System") (CES) of [the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints") (LDS Church).

BYU offers a variety of academic programs including those in the [liberal arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_arts "Liberal arts"), [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_education "Engineering education"), [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), [management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Management "Management"), [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_science "Physical science") and [mathematical sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_sciences "Mathematical sciences"), nursing, music, and law. Its undergraduate and graduate programs are organized into 11 colleges and schools at its main Provo campus, with some colleges and divisions defining their own admission standards. The university also administers four satellite campuses in [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Jerusalem_Center "BYU Jerusalem Center"), [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Salt_Lake_Center "BYU Salt Lake Center"), [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Barlow_Center "BYU Barlow Center"), and [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_London_Study_Abroad_Centre "BYU London Study Abroad Centre"), while its parent organization, CES, sponsors sister schools in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University%E2%80%93Hawaii "Brigham Young University–Hawaii") and [Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University%E2%80%93Idaho "Brigham Young University–Idaho"). The university is accredited by the [Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Commission_on_Colleges_and_Universities "Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities") and is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research spending and doctorate production".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-10)

Almost all BYU students are members of the LDS Church. Students attending BYU agree to follow an [honor code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Educational_System_Honor_Code "Church Educational System Honor Code"), which mandates behavior in line with teachings of the church, such as academic honesty, adherence to dress and grooming standards and abstinence from [extramarital sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexuality_and_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "Sexuality and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints"), [same-sex romantic behavior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality_and_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "Homosexuality and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints"), and [consumption of alcohol and other drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_of_Wisdom_(Latter_Day_Saints) "Word of Wisdom (Latter Day Saints)"). Undergraduate students are also required to complete curriculum in LDS religious education for graduation regardless of their course of study. Due in part to the church's emphasis on [missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mormon_missionary "Mormon missionary") service, nearly 50% of BYU students have lived outside the United States, 65% speak a second language, and 63 languages are taught at the university regularly.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-FF-11)

BYU's athletic teams compete in [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") of the [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") and are collectively known as the [BYU Cougars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Cougars "BYU Cougars"). All sports teams compete in the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") except for men's volleyball which is a member of the [Mountain Pacific Sports Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Pacific_Sports_Federation "Mountain Pacific Sports Federation"). BYU's sports teams have won a total of 14 NCAA championships and 26 non-NCAA championships.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of Brigham Young University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Brigham_Young_University "History of Brigham Young University")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Charles_William_Carter_-_Brigham_Young_-_Google_Art_Project_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg/250px-Charles_William_Carter_-_Brigham_Young_-_Google_Art_Project_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_William_Carter_-_Brigham_Young_-_Google_Art_Project_(3x4_cropped).jpg)

[Brigham Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young "Brigham Young"), the school's [eponym](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/eponym "wikt:eponym")

### Early days

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early days")]

The origin of BYU can be traced back to 1862, when [Warren Dusenberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Newton_Dusenberry "Warren Newton Dusenberry") started a Provo school in Cluff Hall, a prominent adobe building in the northeast corner of 200 East and 200 North.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-12) After some financial difficulties, the school was recreated in the Kinsey and Lewis buildings on Center Street in Provo, and after gaining some recognition for its quality, was adopted to become the Timpanogos branch of the [University of Deseret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Deseret "University of Deseret"). When financial difficulty forced another closure, on October 16, 1875, [Brigham Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young "Brigham Young"), then [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Church_(LDS_Church) "President of the Church (LDS Church)") of the LDS Church, deeded the property to trustees to create _Brigham Young Academy_ after earlier hinting a school would be built in [Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draper,_Utah "Draper, Utah"), Utah, in 1867.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-13) Hence, October 16, 1875, is commonly held as BYU's founding date.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-history-14) Young had been envisioning for several years the concept of a church university.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-15) Said Young about his vision: "I hope to see an Academy established in Provo... at which the children of the Latter-day Saints can receive a good education unmixed with the pernicious atheistic influences that are found in so many of the higher schools of the country."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-dusenberry-16)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Brigham_Young_Academy.jpg/250px-Brigham_Young_Academy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brigham_Young_Academy.jpg)

The Brigham Young Academy building c.1900

Classes at Brigham Young Academy[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-dusenberry-16) commenced on January 3, 1876. Dusenberry served as interim principal for several months until April 1876, when Brigham Young's choice for principal arrived—a German immigrant named [Karl Maeser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_G._Maeser "Karl G. Maeser").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-history-14) During this period the future U.S. Supreme Court Justice [George Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Sutherland "George Sutherland") and future U.S. Senator [Reed Smoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_Smoot "Reed Smoot") attended. The school did not become a university until the end of [Benjamin Cluff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Cluff "Benjamin Cluff")'s term as president in 1903. At that time, the school was still privately supported by members of the community and was not absorbed and sponsored officially by the church until July 18, 1896.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byhigh-17) A series of odd managerial decisions by Cluff led to his demotion; however, in his last official act, he proposed to the board that the academy be named "Brigham Young University." Many opposed, saying the school was not large enough to be a university, but the decision ultimately passed.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-wilk-18)

In 1903, Brigham Young Academy was dissolved and replaced by two institutions, [Brigham Young High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_High_School "Brigham Young High School") (BY High) and BYU.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byhigh-17) The BY High class of 1907 was ultimately responsible for the [giant "Y"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y_Mountain "Y Mountain") that remains embedded on a mountain near campus.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byhigh-17) The Board elected [George H. Brimhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._Brimhall "George H. Brimhall") as the new President of BYU.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-wilk-18) Under his tenure in 1904, the new BYU bought 17 acres (69,000 m 2) of land from Provo called "Temple Hill".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byhigh-17) After some controversy among locals over BYU's purchase of this property, construction began in 1909 on the first building on the current campus, the Karl G. Maeser Memorial.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-19) Brimhall also presided over BYU during a brief crisis involving the theory of evolution. The religious nature of the school seemed at the time to collide with this scientific theory. [Joseph F. Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_F._Smith "Joseph F. Smith"), church president at the time, settled the question for a time by asking that evolution not be taught at the school. Over time, students and faculty found a way to reconcile the factual elements of evolution with the church's teachings.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-evolution-20) Even though a few at this time described the school as little more than a "religious seminary", many of its graduates from this time would go on to great success and become well renowned in a variety of fields.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-wilk-18)

### Expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansion")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Smoot_Building.jpg/250px-Smoot_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Smoot_Building.jpg)

The Abraham O. Smoot Administration Building

In 1921, [Franklin S. Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_S._Harris "Franklin S. Harris") was appointed as BYU's president and was the first in this role to have a doctoral degree. Harris made several significant changes to the school, reorganizing it into a true university, whereas before, its organization had remnants of the academy days. At the beginning of his tenure, the school was not officially recognized as a university by any accreditation organization. By the end of his term, the school was accredited by all major accrediting organizations at the time. He was succeeded by [Howard S. McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._McDonald "Howard S. McDonald"), who received a doctorate from the [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"). When he first received the position, the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") had just ended, and thousands of students were flooding into BYU. By the end of his stay, the school had grown nearly five times to 5,440 students. BYU did not have the facilities to handle such a large influx, so he bought part of an Air Force Base in [Ogden, Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden,_Utah "Ogden, Utah") and rebuilt it to house some of the students.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-wilk-18) The next president, [Ernest L. Wilkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_L._Wilkinson "Ernest L. Wilkinson"), also oversaw a period of intense growth as the school adopted an accelerated building program. Wilkinson was responsible for the building of over eighty structures on the campus, many of which still stand.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-ernest-21) During his tenure, the student body increased six-fold, making BYU the largest private school at the time. The quality of the students also increased, leading to higher educational standards at the school.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-wilk-18) Finally, Wilkinson reorganized LDS Church units on campus, with ten [stakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stake_(Latter_Day_Saints) "Stake (Latter Day Saints)") and over 100 [wards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_(LDS_Church) "Ward (LDS Church)") added during his administration.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-ernest-21)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/BYU_Campus_North.jpg/250px-BYU_Campus_North.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BYU_Campus_North.jpg)

Overlooking North Campus

[Dallin H. Oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallin_H._Oaks "Dallin H. Oaks") replaced Wilkinson as president in 1971. Oaks continued the expansion of his predecessor, adding a law school and proposing plans for a new School of Management. During his administration, a new library was also added, doubling the library space on campus.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-22)[Jeffrey R. Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_R._Holland "Jeffrey R. Holland") followed as president in 1980, encouraging a combination of educational excellence and religious faith. He believed one of the school's greatest strengths was its religious nature and that this should be taken advantage of, rather than hidden. During his administration, BYU added a campus in Jerusalem, now called the [BYU Jerusalem Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Jerusalem_Center "BYU Jerusalem Center"). In 1989, Holland was replaced by [Rex E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_E._Lee "Rex E. Lee").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-23) Lee was responsible for the construction of the Benson Science Building and the Museum of Art.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-24) A cancer victim, Lee is memorialized annually at BYU during a cancer fundraiser called the Rex Lee Run.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-25) Shortly before his death, Lee resigned and was replaced in 1995 by [Merrill J. Bateman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_J._Bateman "Merrill J. Bateman").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-26)

Bateman was responsible for the construction of 36 new buildings for BYU, both on and off the campus, including the expansion of the Harold B. Lee Library. He was also one of several key college leaders who brought about the creation of the [Mountain West Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_West_Conference "Mountain West Conference"), which BYU's athletics program joined — BYU previously participated in the [Western Athletic Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Athletic_Conference "Western Athletic Conference"). A [satellite TV network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_TV "BYU TV") also opened in 2000 under his leadership.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-27) Bateman was followed by [Cecil O. Samuelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_O._Samuelson "Cecil O. Samuelson") in 2003.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-28) Samuelson was succeeded by [Kevin J Worthen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_J_Worthen "Kevin J Worthen") in 2014.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-deseretnews.com-29)[C. Shane Reese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Shane_Reese "C. Shane Reese") became BYU's 14th president on May 1, 2023.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-30) On July 29, 2024, the First Presidency of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced plans to create a medical school for the university.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-31)

In 2025, the university was declared an [undesirable organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_undesirable_organizations_law "Russian undesirable organizations law") in Russia.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-32)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Campus")]

Main articles: [Brigham Young University campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_campus "Brigham Young University campus") and [List of Brigham Young University buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Brigham_Young_University_buildings "List of Brigham Young University buildings")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/BYU_mountain_view.JPG/250px-BYU_mountain_view.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BYU_mountain_view.JPG)

BYU campus with Y mountain and [Kyhv Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyhv_Peak "Kyhv Peak") (formerly called Squaw Peak) in the background

The main campus in [Provo, Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provo,_Utah "Provo, Utah"), sits on approximately 560 acres (2.3 km 2) nestled at the base of the [Wasatch Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasatch_Mountains "Wasatch Mountains") and includes 295 buildings.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byucampus-33) The buildings feature a wide variety of architectural styles, each building being built in the style of its time.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langvalue-34) Views of the Wasatch Mountains, (including [Mount Timpanogos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Timpanogos "Mount Timpanogos")) can be seen from the campus.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byucampus-33) BYU's [Harold B. Lee Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_B._Lee_Library "Harold B. Lee Library") (also known as "HBLL"), which _[The Princeton Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Princeton\_Review "The Princeton Review")_ ranked as the No. 1 "Great College Library" in 2004,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-35) has approximately 8.5 million items in its collections, contains 98 miles (158 km) of shelving, and can seat 4,600 people.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-36) The [Spencer W. Kimball Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_W._Kimball_Tower "Spencer W. Kimball Tower") is home to several of the university's departments and programs and for a long time was the tallest building in Provo, Utah,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Emporis-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-BYUPage-38) and the [Marriott Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriott_Center "Marriott Center") serves primarily as a basketball arena and can seat over 19,000, making it the tenth largest on-campus arena in the nation.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-39) On Sundays, nearly all of the buildings on campus are utilized to host church services.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Sunday_at_School-41)

### Museums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Museums")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/MOA_North_entrance.JPG/250px-MOA_North_entrance.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MOA_North_entrance.JPG)

[Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Museum_of_Art "Brigham Young University Museum of Art") north entrance

Several museums on campus contain exhibits from many different fields of study. BYU's [Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Museum_of_Art "Brigham Young University Museum of Art"), for example, is one of the largest and most attended art museums in the Mountain West. This museum offers research and study opportunities to students and educational programming to the general public.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-42) The [Museum of Peoples and Cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Museum_of_Peoples_and_Cultures "Brigham Young University Museum of Peoples and Cultures") is a museum of archaeology and ethnology. It focuses on native cultures and artifacts of the Great Basin, American Southwest, Mesoamerica, Peru, and Polynesia. Home to more than 40,000 artifacts and 50,000 photographs, it documents BYU's archaeological research.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-43) The [BYU Museum of Paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Museum_of_Paleontology "BYU Museum of Paleontology")[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-44) was built in 1976 to display the many fossils found by BYU's [James A. Jensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_A._Jensen "James A. Jensen"). It holds many vertebrate fossils from the [Jurassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic_Period "Jurassic Period") and Cretaceous periods and is one of the top five vertebrate fossil collections in the world from the Jurassic.  The museum receives about 25,000 visitors every year.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-46) The [Monte L. Bean Life Science Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_L._Bean_Life_Science_Museum "Monte L. Bean Life Science Museum") was formed in 1978. It features several forms of plant and animal life on display and available for research by students and scholars.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-47)

### Performing arts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Performing arts")]

The campus also houses several performing arts facilities. The de Jong Concert Hall seats 1282 people and is named for [Gerrit de Jong Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrit_de_Jong_Jr. "Gerrit de Jong Jr.") The Pardoe Theatre is named for T. Earl and Kathryn Pardoe. Students use its stage in a variety of theatre experiments, as well as for Pardoe Series performances. It seats 500 people, and has quite a large stage with a [proscenium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proscenium "Proscenium") opening of 19 by 55 feet (17 m).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byutheater-48) The Margetts Theatre was named for Philip N. Margetts, a prominent Utah theatre figure. A smaller, [black box theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_box_theater "Black box theater"), it allows a variety of seating and staging formats. It seats 125, and measures 30 by 50 feet (15 m).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byutheater-48) The Nelke Theatre, named for one of BYU's first drama teachers, is used largely for instruction in experimental theater. It seats 280.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byutheater-48)

### Student housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Student housing")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/ForeignLanguageHousing.JPG/250px-ForeignLanguageHousing.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ForeignLanguageHousing.JPG)

Foreign Language Student Residence, where students commit to speak only their language of study

BYU has on-campus housing communities for freshmen students as well as for students 19 years and older. Single students who are freshmen have four options for on-campus housing: Heritage Halls, Helaman Halls, Riviera Apartments, and the Foreign Language Student Residence (FLSR). On-campus housing for single students 19 years old and older is available at Wyview Park, Heritage Halls, and in the Foreign Language Student Residence Halls. On-campus married students live in Wymount Terrace or Wyview Park.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-49)

### BYU Creamery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: BYU Creamery")]

Branches of the BYU Creamery provide basic food and general grocery products for students living in Heritage Halls, Helaman, Wymount, Wyview, and the Foreign Language Student Residence. Helaman Halls is also served by a central cafeteria called the Cannon Center.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byurooms-50) The Creamery on Ninth East opened in August 2000, replacing Kent's Market, which closed during the 1998–1999 school year.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byunews-51) BYU's building block system [abbreviates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbreviation "Abbreviation") the Creamery on Ninth East as CONE.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byunews-51)

The creamery began in 1949 to provide milk for the campus, and soon thereafter it expanded its product line to include ice cream, cheeses, and other University-produced [dairy products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dairy_product "Dairy product"). It has become a BYU tradition and is also frequented by visitors to the university and members of the community.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-52) It was the first on-campus full-service grocery store in the country.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-53)

According to the BYU Dining Services statistics, more than 191,000 gallons of Creamery ice cream are served each year.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-54) In 2018, in celebration of being named most "Stone Cold Sober" school for twenty-one straight years by the Princeton Review, BYU Creamery released a new flavor of milk, mint brownie chocolate milk.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-55)

### Sustainability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Sustainability")]

BYU has designated energy conservation, products and materials, recycling, site planning and building design, student involvement, transportation, water conservation, and zero waste events as top priority categories. The university has stated "we have a responsibility to be wise stewards of the earth and its resources."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Y_Facts_-_Sustainability-56) BYU is working to increase the energy efficiency of its buildings by installing various speed drives on all pumps and fans, replacing incandescent lighting with fluorescent lighting, retrofitting campus buildings with low-E reflective glass, and upgraded roof insulation to prevent heat loss.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Energy_Conservation-57) BYU Recycles spearheaded the recent campaign to begin recycling plastics, which the university did after a year of student campaigning.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Student_Involvement-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-BYU_Newsnet_-_Going_Toward_the_Green-59)

BYU is a part of CES. It is organized under a [board of trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_trustees "Board of trustees"), with the president of the church (currently [Dallin H. Oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallin_H._Oaks "Dallin H. Oaks")) as chairman. This board consists of the same people as the [Church Board of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Education_System#Church_Board_of_Education_and_Boards_of_Trustees "Church Education System"), a pattern that has been in place since 1939. Prior to 1939, BYU had a separate board of trustees that was subordinate to the Church Board of Education.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-61) The president of BYU, currently C. Shane Reese, reports to the Board, through the Commissioner of Education.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-62)

The university operates under 11 colleges or schools, which collectively offer 194 bachelor's degree programs, 68 master's degree programs, 25 PhD programs, and a [Juris Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") program. Kennedy Center for International Studies") and "miscellaneous" college departments, including Undergraduate Education, Graduate Studies, Independent Study,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-63) Continuing Education, and the Honors Program. BYU's Winter semester ends earlier than most universities in April since there is no [Spring break](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_break "Spring break"), thus allowing students to pursue internships and other summer activities earlier.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-64) A typical academic year is broken up into two semesters: Fall (September–December) and Winter (January–April), as well as two shorter terms during the summer months: Spring (May–June) and Summer (July–August).

### Admissions and demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Admissions and demographics")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Harold_B._Lee_Library.jpg/250px-Harold_B._Lee_Library.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harold_B._Lee_Library.jpg)

The [Harold B. Lee Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_B._Lee_Library "Harold B. Lee Library") is consistently ranked among the top ten in the nation, with a No. 1 ranking in 2004 by _[The Princeton Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Princeton\_Review "The Princeton Review")_.

Of the 14,067 freshman students that applied, BYU accepted 70.2% of them. [[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Entrance-65) The average GPA for these admitted students was 3.86 with an average [ACT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_(test) "ACT (test)") of 29.5 and [SAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT") of 1300.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Entrance-65) In 2004, a [National Bureau of Economic Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Economic_Research "National Bureau of Economic Research") study on revealed preference of U.S. colleges showed BYU was the 6th most-preferred choice in the [Intermountain West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermountain_West "Intermountain West"), between Princeton and Brown.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-66) Students from every state in the U.S. and from many foreign countries attend BYU. (In the 2005–06 academic year, there were 2,396 foreign students, or eight percent of enrollment.)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-chronicle-67) Slightly more than 98 percent of these students are active Latter-day Saints. In 2006, 12.6 percent of the student body reported themselves as ethnic minorities, mostly Asians, Pacific Islanders and Hispanics.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-68) In 2025, the racial breakdown of students was 80.6% white, 9.3% Hispanic or Latino, 4.5% multi-ethnic, 3% Asian, 1% Black, 1% native Hawaiian, and less than 1% American Indian.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-69) The racial composition of students at BYU is mostly [non-Hispanic white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Hispanic_or_Latino_whites "Non-Hispanic or Latino whites"), and BYU is considered one of the least diverse of the top 100 universities in the United States.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-70)

The BYU [J. Reuben Clark Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Reuben_Clark_Law_School "J. Reuben Clark Law School") has a No. 24 (tie) national ranking for 2026, according to _U.S. News & World Report_.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-79)

### Graduation honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Graduation honors")]

Undergraduate students may qualify for graduation honors. _University Honors_ is the highest distinction BYU awards its graduates.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-80) Administered by the [Honors Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Honors_Program "Brigham Young University Honors Program"), the distinction requires students to complete an honors curriculum requirement, a Great Questions requirement, an Experiential Learning requirement, an honors thesis requirement, and a graduation portfolio that summarizes the student's honors experiences.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-81)

The university also awards [Latin scholastic distinctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_honors "Latin honors") separately from the Honors Program: summa cum laude (top 1 percent), magna cum laude (top 5 percent), and cum laude (top 10 percent).[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-honors-82) The university additionally recognizes [Phi Kappa Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Kappa_Phi "Phi Kappa Phi") graduation honors.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-83)

"Domo, Inc."), [Novell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novell "Novell"), [Nu Skin Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu_Skin_Enterprises "Nu Skin Enterprises"), [Qualtrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualtrics "Qualtrics"), [Pluralsight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluralsight "Pluralsight"), [The Trade Desk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Trade_Desk "The Trade Desk"), and [Vivint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivint "Vivint").

### Devotionals and forums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Devotionals and forums")]

To provide students with opportunities for both spiritual and intellectual insight, BYU has hosted weekly devotional and forum assemblies since the school's early days.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-97) Devotionals are most common and address religious topics, often with academic perspective or insight. Devotional speakers are typically drawn from the BYU faculty and administration or LDS Church leadership, including church presidents George Albert Smith, Spencer W. Kimball, Thomas S. Monson, and Russell M. Nelson.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-98)

Several times each year the devotional is replaced by a forum, which typically addresses a more secular topic and may include a speaker from outside the BYU or Latter-day Saint community. In recent years, forum speakers have included notable politicians (e.g. Joseph Lieberman, Mitt Romney), scientists (Neil deGrasse Tyson, DJ Patil), historians (David McCullough, Richard Beeman), religious leaders (Archbishop Charles Chaput, Albert Mohler) and judicial figures (John Roberts, Thomas Griffith).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Although attendance is not required, several thousand students attend the weekly assemblies, which are also broadcast on BYUtv[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-99) and archived in text, audio, and video formats on the BYU Speeches website.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-100)

### International focus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: International focus")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/ESC_Eyring_Science_Center.jpg/250px-ESC_Eyring_Science_Center.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ESC_Eyring_Science_Center.jpg)

The [Eyring Science Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyring_Science_Center "Eyring Science Center") houses a [planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetarium "Planetarium"), an [anechoic chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anechoic_chamber "Anechoic chamber") and a [Foucault pendulum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foucault_pendulum "Foucault pendulum").

Over three quarters of the student body has some proficiency in a second language (numbering 107 languages in total).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langfact-101) This is partially because 45 percent of the student body at BYU have been Latter-day Saint [missionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary_(LDS_Church) "Missionary (LDS Church)"), and many of them learned a foreign language as part of their mission assignment.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-102) During any given semester, about one-third of the student body is enrolled in foreign language classes, a rate nearly four times the national average.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langfact-101) BYU offers courses in over 60 different languages,[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langfact-101) many with advanced courses that are seldom offered elsewhere. Several of its language programs are the largest of their type in the nation, such as the Russian program.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langvalue-34) The university was selected by the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") as the location of the national Middle East Language Resource Center, making the school a hub for experts on that region.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langvalue-34) It was also selected as a Center for International Business Education Research, a function of which is to train business employees in international languages and relations.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-langfact-101)

Beyond this, BYU also runs a very large study abroad program, with satellite centers in London, [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Jerusalem_Center "BYU Jerusalem Center"), and Paris, as well as more than 20 other sites.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-103) Nearly 2,000 students take advantage of these programs yearly. In 2001, the [Institute of International Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_International_Education "Institute of International Education") ranked BYU as the number one university in the U.S. to offer students study abroad opportunities.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-105) The [BYU Jerusalem Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Jerusalem_Center "BYU Jerusalem Center"), which was closed in 2000 due to student security concerns related to the [Second Intifada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Intifada "Second Intifada") and later the [2006 Israel-Lebanon conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Israel-Lebanon_conflict "2006 Israel-Lebanon conflict"), was reopened to students in the Winter 2007 semester.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-106)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/MaeserBuilding.JPG/250px-MaeserBuilding.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MaeserBuilding.JPG)

The Maeser Building, built in 1911, houses [BYU's Honors Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Honors_Program "Brigham Young University Honors Program").

A few special additions enhance the language-learning experience. For example, BYU's International Cinema, featuring films in several languages, is the largest and longest-running university-run foreign film program in the country.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-107) BYU also offers an intensive foreign language living experience, the Foreign Language Student Residence. This is an on-campus apartment complex where students commit to speak only their chosen foreign language while in their apartments. Each apartment has at least one native speaker to ensure correct language usage.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-108)

### Academic freedom issues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Academic freedom issues")]

Main article: [Academic freedom at Brigham Young University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_freedom_at_Brigham_Young_University "Academic freedom at Brigham Young University")

In 1992, the university drafted a new Statement on Academic Freedom,[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-acadfree-109) specifying that limitations may be placed upon "expression with students or in public that: (1) contradicts or opposes, rather than analyzes or discusses, fundamental Latter-day Saint doctrine or policy; (2) deliberately attacks or derides the church or its general leaders; or (3) violates the [Honor Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Honor_Code "Brigham Young University Honor Code") because the expression is dishonest, illegal, unchaste, profane, or unduly disrespectful of others." These restrictions caused some controversy as several professors had been disciplined according to the then-new rule. The [American Association of University Professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_of_University_Professors "American Association of University Professors") (AAUP) had claimed that "infringements on academic freedom are distressingly common and that the climate for academic freedom is distressingly poor."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-aaupreport-110) The newer rules have not affected BYU's accreditation, as the university's chosen accrediting body allows "religious colleges and universities to place limitations on academic freedom so long as they publish those limitations candidly", according to associate academic vice president Jim Gordon.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-NascuOnAcademicFreedom-111) The AAUP's concern was not with restrictions on the faculty member's religious expression but with a failure, as alleged by the faculty member and AAUP, that the restrictions had not been adequately specified in advance by BYU: "The AAUP requires that any doctrinal limitations on academic freedom be laid out clearly in writing. We [AAUP] concluded that BYU had failed to do so adequately."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-112)

In 2021, _[The Salt Lake Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Salt\_Lake\_Tribune "The Salt Lake Tribune")_ noted the tension between faith and scholarship that has existed at the university as early as 1910, and how the recent LDS Church calls for a retrenchment has some BYU professors worried about a new wave of [fideism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fideism "Fideism") at the university.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-The_Salt_Lake_Tribune_2021-113) According to a third-party survey that allowed faculty to answer anonymously, more than 90 percent of BYU faculty said they were satisfied or very satisfied with their jobs.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-114)

### Dance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Dance")]

The [BYU Ballroom Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Ballroom_Dance_Company "BYU Ballroom Dance Company") is known as one of the best formation ballroom dance teams in the world,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-115) having won the U.S. National Formation Dance Championship every year since 1982.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-dancetwo-116) BYU's ballroom dance team has won first place in Latin or Standard (or both) many times when they have competed at the [Blackpool Dance Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpool_Dance_Festival "Blackpool Dance Festival"), and they were the first U.S. team to win the formation championships at the famed British Championships in Blackpool, England in 1972.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-dance-117) The NDCA National [DanceSport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DanceSport "DanceSport") championships have been held at BYU for several years, and BYU holds dozens of ballroom dance classes each semester and has consequently the largest collegiate ballroom dance program in the world.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-dancetwo-116) In addition, BYU has a number of other notable dance teams and programs. These teams include the Theatre Ballet, Contemporary Dance Theatre, Living Legends, and International Folk Dance Ensemble. The Living Legends perform Latin, Native American, and Polynesian dancing. BYU boasts one of the largest dance departments in the nation. Many students from all different majors across campus participate in various dance classes each semester.

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [BYU Cougars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYU_Cougars "BYU Cougars")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/BYA_Football_Champions_1896.png/250px-BYA_Football_Champions_1896.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BYA_Football_Champions_1896.png)

The school's first football team, which won the regional championship in 1896

BYU sponsors 21 athletic teams that compete in [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") of the [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association"), plus 6 teams that compete in extramural competition and over 50 intramural activities.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-byucougars1-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-125) All sports teams compete in the [Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") except for men's volleyball which is a member of the [Mountain Pacific Sports Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Pacific_Sports_Federation "Mountain Pacific Sports Federation"). BYU's sports teams have won a total of 14 NCAA championships and 26 non-NCAA championships. In 2021, BYU formally accepted an invitation to the Big 12 Conference and started participating in the conference in the 2023–24 school year.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Big12-126) Also that year, BYU's athletics program was ranked #17 out of 293 Division I schools for overall athletics by the [National Association of Collegiate Directors of Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Collegiate_Directors_of_Athletics "National Association of Collegiate Directors of Athletics") ([Directors' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACDA_Directors'_Cup "NACDA Directors' Cup")).[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-127)

BYU's athletic teams are named the "Cougars", with [Cosmo the Cougar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmo_the_Cougar "Cosmo the Cougar") serving as the school's mascot since 1953. The school's fight song is the [Cougar Fight Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cougar_Song_(BYU) "The Cougar Song (BYU)"). Because many of its players serve on full-time missions for two years (men when they are 18, women when 19), BYU athletes are often older on average than other schools' players. The NCAA allows students to serve missions for two years without subtracting that time from their eligibility period. This has caused minor controversy, but is largely recognized as not lending the school any significant advantage, since players receive no athletic and little physical training during their missions.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-128) BYU has also received attention from sports networks for refusal to play games on Sunday, as well as [expelling players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_BYU_Cougars_men's_basketball_team#Davies_controversy "2010–11 BYU Cougars men's basketball team") due to honor code violations.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-129)

The university's teams and individual players have won various awards for their achievements. Its football has had seven inductees into the [College Football Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_Hall_of_Fame "College Football Hall of Fame") and one [Heisman Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heisman_Trophy "Heisman Trophy") winner, and it claims the [National Championship in 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_BYU_Cougars_football_team "1984 BYU Cougars football team").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-130) In basketball, BYU has had several standout basketball players including 2011 [Naismith College Player of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naismith_College_Player_of_the_Year "Naismith College Player of the Year")[Jimmer Fredette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmer_Fredette "Jimmer Fredette") and 1981 [John R. Wooden Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Wooden_Award "John R. Wooden Award") winner [Danny Ainge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Ainge "Danny Ainge").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-ESPN.com-131)

## Student life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Student life")]

### Religious atmosphere

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Religious atmosphere")]

BYU's stated mission "is to assist individuals in their quest for perfection and [eternal life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exaltation_(LDS_Church) "Exaltation (LDS Church)")." BYU is thus considered by its leaders to be at heart a religious institution, wherein, ideally, religious and secular education are interwoven in a way that encourages the highest standards in both areas.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Peer-132) This weaving of the secular and the religious aspects of a religious university goes back as far as Brigham Young himself, who told Karl G. Maeser when the church purchased the school: "I want you to remember that you ought not to teach even the alphabet or the multiplication tables without the [Spirit of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit_in_Christianity#The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints "Holy Spirit in Christianity")."[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-133)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-134)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/BYU_Bell_Tower_with_Provo_Temple.JPG/250px-BYU_Bell_Tower_with_Provo_Temple.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BYU_Bell_Tower_with_Provo_Temple.JPG)

The [BYU Bell Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_Centennial_Carillon_Tower "Brigham Young University Centennial Carillon Tower") with the [Provo Utah Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provo_Utah_Temple "Provo Utah Temple") in the background

BYU has been considered by some Latter-day Saints, as well as some university and church leaders, to be "The Lord's university". This phrase is used in reference to the school's mission as an ambassador to the world for the Church of Jesus Christ, and thus for [Jesus Christ in Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_in_Christianity "Jesus in Christianity").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Peer-132)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-135) In the past, some students and faculty have expressed dissatisfaction with this nickname, stating that it gives students the idea that university authorities are always divinely inspired and never to be contradicted.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-136) Leaders of the school, however, acknowledge that the nickname represents more a goal that the university strives for and not its current state of being. Leaders encourage students and faculty to help fulfill the goal by following the teachings of their religion, adhering to the school's honor code, and serving others with the knowledge they gain while attending.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-137)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-138)

BYU mandates that its students who are Latter-day Saints be religiously active.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-139) All applicants are required to provide an endorsement from an ecclesiastic leader with their application for admittance.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-ecclestical-140) Over 900 rooms on the BYU campus are used for the purposes of Church congregations. More than 150 congregations meet on BYU campus each Sunday, where "BYU's campus becomes one of the busiest and largest centers of worship in the world" with about 24,000 persons attending church services on campus.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-141)

Some 97 percent of male BYU graduates and 32 percent of female graduates have served as Latter-day Saint missionaries.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-142) In October 2012, the church announced at its general conference that young men could serve a mission after they turn 18 and have graduated from high school. Since that time many young men have elected to enroll at BYU after their mission rather than taking a hiatus during their college studies. Missionary service often lasts up to two years for young men, and up to 18 months for young women.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-mission-143)

### Honor code

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Honor code")]

Main article: [Church Educational System Honor Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Educational_System_Honor_Code "Church Educational System Honor Code")

...Each member of the BYU community personally commits to observe these Honor Code standards approved by the Board of Trustees "at all times and in all things, and in all places" (Mosiah 18:9):

*   Be honest.
*   Live a chaste and virtuous life, including abstaining from any sexual relations outside a marriage between a man and a woman.
*   Respect others, including the avoidance of profane and vulgar language.
*   Obey the law and follow campus policies.
*   Abstain from alcoholic beverages, tobacco, tea, coffee, vaping, and substance abuse.
*   Participate regularly in Church services (required only of Church members).
*   Observe Brigham Young University's Dress and Grooming Standards.
*   Encourage others in their commitment to comply with the Honor Code.
— Church Educational System Honor Code Statement[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-CESHonorCode-144)

All students and faculty, regardless of religion, are required to agree to adhere to an [honor code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_honor_code "Academic honor code"). Early forms of the CES Honor Code are found as far back as the days of the Brigham Young Academy and early school President Karl G. Maeser. Maeser created the "Domestic Organization", a group of teachers who would visit students at their homes to ensure they were following the school's moral rules prohibiting obscenity, profanity, smoking, and alcohol consumption. The Honor Code was not formally created until about 1940, and was initially used mainly for cases of cheating and [academic dishonesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_dishonesty "Academic dishonesty").

President Wilkinson expanded the Honor Code in 1957 to include other school standards. This led to what the Honor Code represents today: rules regarding chastity, dress, grooming, drugs, and alcohol. A signed commitment to live the honor code is part of the application process, and must be adhered by all students, faculty, and staff. Students and faculty found in violation of standards are warned or called to meet with representatives of the Honor Council. In certain cases, students and faculty can be expelled or lose tenure. All students, regardless of religious affiliation or Church membership, are required to meet annually with a Church or other religious leader to receive an ecclesiastical endorsement for both acceptance and continuance at the university.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-BYUhouse3-145)

#### Policies around LGBTQ students

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Policies around LGBTQ students")]

Main article: [Brigham Young University LGBTQ history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University_LGBTQ_history "Brigham Young University LGBTQ history")

See also: [Timeline of BYU LGBTQ history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_BYU_LGBTQ_history "Timeline of BYU LGBTQ history")

BYU has regularly been ranked among the least [LGBTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ")-friendly schools in the United States[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-146)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-148) and its policies towards LGBTQ students have sparked criticism and protests.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-149)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-150)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-151) It continues to ban same-sex romantic behavior such as dating, holding hands, and kissing as of August 2023.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-152)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-153) Historically, experiences for BYU students identifying as LGBTQ have included being banned from enrolling due to their romantic attractions in the 60s,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Dynamics-154):379 being required by school administration to undergo electroshock and vomit aversion therapies in the 1970s,[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Multiply-155):155 having nearly 80% of BYU students reporting they'd refuse to live with an openly homosexual person in a poll in the 1990s,[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Ban-156) and a campus-wide ban on coming out until 2007.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Century-157)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Ask-158)

Until 2021, there were not any LGBTQ–specific resources on campus, though there is now the Office of Student Success and Inclusion.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Inside-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-USA_Today-160)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Blade-161) Though the ban on coming out was lifted in 2007, LGBTQ BYU students are at risk of expulsion for any same-sex romantic expression including hugging and handholding.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Ban-156)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Wings-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Stinging-163) Before 2021, queer students were banned from meeting together in an [LGBTQ–straight alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay%E2%80%93straight_alliance "Gay–straight alliance") group on-campus.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Assault-164)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Struggles-165)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-Decided-166)

#### Effects on sexual assault reporting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brigham_Young_University&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Effects on sexual assault reporting")]

Beginning in 2014 and continuing through 2016, some students reported that, after being sexually assaulted or raped, they were told they would face discipline because of honor code violations for consensual sexual relationships in violation of the policy that came to light during the investigation of reported sexual assaults.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-:4-167)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-168) Criticism has been leveled that this atmosphere may prevent other students from reporting sexual assault crimes to police, a situation that local law enforcement have publicly criticized.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-169) In response, the Victim Services Coordinator of the Provo Police Department called for an amnesty clause to be added to the Honor Code, which would not punish sexual assault survivors for past honor code violations discovered during the investigation.

In 2016 and 2017 the Honor Code, in light of identified potential conflicts with [Title IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_IX "Title IX") obligations, was extensively reviewed and updated.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-170) As a result of a review, which concluded in October 2016, BYU announced several changes to how it would handle sexual assault reports, including adding an amnesty clause, and ensuring under most circumstances that information is not shared between Title IX Office and Honor Code Office without the victim's consent.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-KUTV_changes-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-:1-172) In June 2017, the policy was further revised to affirm that "BYU strongly encourages the reporting of all incidents of sexual misconduct so that support services can be offered to victims and sexual misconduct can be prevented and stopped".[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-:0-173) Current policy assures that victims "will not be disciplined by the university for any related honor code violation occurring at or near the time of the reported sexual misconduct unless a person's health or safety is at risk."[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-:0-173)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University#cite_note-174)
